newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian government pledges privatisation, reform.
newsitem.headline: Serbian government pledges privatisation, reform.

text.p: The Serbian government, in an abrupt change of its economic stance, has promised its people a year of privatisation and reform.
Economists welcomed the reversal but cautioned that any privatisation and transition to a market economy will mean little without substantial financial backing from abroad.

"The coming year will be a year of reforms -- major ownership and structural changes, which should make possible an affirmation of all motivating elements in a market economy," Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic said.
In a New Year's message broadcast by state television, he also announced the launch of major projects "which will change the face of our country".
Yugoslav deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic said earlier that privatisation was a concept of development.
"I expect already at the beginning of the year that we will see tremendous progress in those activities in the basic infrastructure, such as telecommunications and power production," he told Reuters.

In December, Sainovic met representatives of the New York-based investment bank Wasserstein Parella & Co and discussed privatisation of major industries but also of medium sized industries such as breweries, cement, tobacco, sugar and confectionery.
"There are no limits. And as I said, economic interest is the driving force for privatisation in Yugoslavia," he said.
Sainovic insisted that Yugoslavia will not repeat mistakes made by other East European countries.
He said Yugoslavia had a new privatisation concept wherein privatisation proceeds will be reinvested in the economy, while state funds will be financed from the usual taxation system.
Economists agreed privatisation was an imperative for the economy to progress, but feared the process could be stalled because of a lack of external funding.

Some analysts also saw possible resistance to privatisation from within the government because some members of the ruling Socialists run lucrative state companies and at the same time occupy important ministerial posts.
"There is an evident conflict of interest, and those ministers must decide whether they want to keep their ministerial post or be only businessmen," an analyst who asked not to be named told Reuters.
Jurij Bajec, chief of the government's team of economic experts, denied that the government itself had been avoiding privatisation.
He said inefficient parts of the economy with big inherited surplus labour feared market principles and competition.

Danko Djunic, head of the Belgrade-based Economics Institute, said the Yugoslav economy had exhausted its capital reserves and changes in the existing ownership structure would bring nothing essential without additional capital.

"But privatisation is needed because the state is a very bad manager, able only to take from the successful and transfer funds to the bad ones for the sake of (social) peace," Djunic said, adding the state should leave business to businessmen.
Djunic, whose institute is engaged in preparing some of the biggest privatisation projects in Serbia, also said the Yugoslav economy must restructure.
Yugoslavia can no longer rely on agriculture and energy for its growth. It must develop the services sector and support export-oriented industries, he said.
Privatisation and restructuring were seen as key to restoring financial discipline in the country where creditors face big problems in collecting debt.

"The government placed currency and price stability at the top of its economic priorities in 1997, but stability depends on how fast financial discipline is established" the Institute for Market Research (IZIT) said in its latest monthly report.
IZIT said stability was not only important for successful, long-term and continuous economic growth, but also crucial to attracting fresh capital.

But to create financial discipline and maintain overall economic stability, the state will have to deal with bad and insolvent companies and banks, the report said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
